summary: This work introduces a post-selection error mitigation technique that measures auxiliary qubits at circuit points where they are expected to return to the $|0\rangle$ state; shots with measurement outcomes inconsistent with the zero state are rejected based on a likelihood model accounting for gate and measurement noise. Simulations on arithmetic circuits compiled by the Classiq platform show a $\sim 10\%$ reduction in false-negative rate while discarding only $\sim 1\%$ of valid shots.
motivation: Auxiliary qubits are ubiquitous in quantum algorithms for entanglement generation and circuit control, and in many designs (particularly compiler-generated arithmetic circuits) they are expected to return to $|0\rangle$ after use; deviations from this behavior indicate circuit-level errors and can inform post-selection.
method: A probabilistic likelihood model estimates $\Pr(\text{no error in lightcone}_i | m_i = 1) \approx \frac{q}{G_i r p + q}$ for each auxiliary measurement by analyzing the backward lightcone of gates (depth $G_i$) that could affect that outcome, accounting for independent gate failure probability $p$, flip probability $r$, and measurement error $q$; shots with $\mathcal{P}(\vec{m}) < \mathcal{P}_{\text{th}}$ are rejected.
result: Mid-circuit validation at all expected auxiliary reset points reduces the false-negative rate by $\sim 10\%$ compared to no validation, with a false-positive overhead (discarded valid shots) of only $\sim 1\%$; validation at the final measurement alone provides intermediate performance, demonstrating the benefit of placement at intermediate reset points with localized backward lightcones.
